title: Founder's bookshelf
note: Distilled by theme from four books, each idea credited to its author: Ready, Fire, Aim (Michael Masterson), The Effective Executive (Peter F. Drucker), The Ideal Team Player (Patrick Lencioni), Scaling People (Claire Hughes Johnson). Written from Claude's knowledge of the books, not yet checked against their text; no outside commentary.

concepts.s: Get a good-enough product to paying customers fast, then perfect it from their response.

x.b:
• Masterson: most new ventures die from waiting, not from imperfect launches. Prepare enough to act (ready), launch and sell (fire), then refine from results (aim).
  • Masterson: speed beats polish early: what customers buy tells you more than any plan.

• Launch when it works, not when it is perfect.
  • Let sales results decide the next version.
Trap: Reading it as no preparation. Ready still comes first.

cards.a: Ready, fire, aim: prepare enough, launch and sell, then refine.
Market response teaches more than planning, and waiting kills ventures.

concepts.s: A business passes four revenue stages, each with one dominant problem the founder must solve before the next.

x.b:
1. Infancy, about $0 to $1M: make the first profitable sale. Everything is selling.
  2. Childhood, about $1M to $10M: innovate: develop many new profitable products fast.
  3. Adolescence, about $10M to $50M: build management, systems and structure.
  4. Adulthood, about $50M to $100M+: keep entrepreneurial speed alive as the company institutionalizes.

• Identify your stage and work only its main problem.
  • Change your own role at each boundary; the skills that won one stage hinder the next.

cards.a: The first profitable sale.
Innovation: many new profitable products quickly.
Management, systems and structure.
Losing entrepreneurial speed to bureaucracy.

concepts.s: Until you can sell profitably, selling is the founder's main job, so find the offer that works before anything else.

x.b:
• Masterson: in stage one, spend most of your time on selling and marketing, not on product, systems or hiring.
  • Masterson: find your Optimal Selling Strategy: the right product, at the right price, sold the right way. Test until one combination produces profitable sales, then scale it.

• Test offers, prices and pitches; keep what sells.
  • Postpone what does not help the next sale.
Trap: Building infrastructure before a profitable sale exists.

cards.q: Founder's main job in stage one?
cards.a: Selling.

cards.q: What is the Optimal Selling Strategy?
cards.a: The right product at the right price, sold the right way, found by testing.

concepts.s: Once the first product sells, growth comes from turning out many new products quickly, each pushed by a champion.

x.b:
• Masterson: in stage two, innovation means many good-enough launches, mostly improvements on what already sells.
  • Masterson: each idea needs a champion who believes in it and has authority to push it; without one it stalls.

• Run many small launches; drop losers fast.
  • Assign every new product one owner.

cards.a: Many quick launches, mostly improvements on what sells.

cards.q: Why does each idea need a champion?
cards.a: Without a committed owner with authority, it stalls.

concepts.s: Time is the scarcest resource, so record where it goes, cut what wastes it, and consolidate what is left.

x.b:
1. Drucker: Record time as it is spent; memory is unreliable.
  2. Manage: cut what need not be done, delegate what others can do, stop wasting others' time.
  3. Consolidate discretionary time into large blocks; knowledge work needs long uninterrupted stretches.
  • Drucker: recurring time-wasters: the same crisis every year (missing system), overstaffing, too many meetings (you either meet or work, not both), and information that arrives too late or in the wrong form.
• Log your time for a few weeks; ask of each item: what if it weren't done at all?

cards.a: Record, manage, consolidate.

cards.q: What does a crisis that recurs each year signal?
cards.a: A missing system or lack of foresight.
You either meet or work; you cannot do both at once.

concepts.s: Ask what you can contribute to the organization's results, not what effort you put in.

x.b:
• Drucker: anyone whose knowledge work affects results is an executive, whatever the title.
  • Drucker: effectiveness, getting the right things done, is a learnable habit.
  • Drucker: contribution has three areas: direct results, building values, developing people for tomorrow.
  • Drucker: asking about contribution produces good human relations: communication, teamwork, self-development, developing others.
• Ask: what can I contribute that would significantly change results?

cards.a: Any knowledge worker whose decisions affect results.
Direct results, values, people development.
Yes; Drucker treats it as a set of habits.

concepts.s: Concentrate on the few most important tasks, one at a time, and deliberately decide what not to do.

x.b:
• Drucker: concentration is the one secret of effectiveness.
  • Drucker: set posteriorities, what to stop or not start; that is harder than setting priorities.
  • Drucker: regularly prune activities from the past that no longer produce.
  • Drucker: choose by future over past, opportunity over problem, your own direction over the bandwagon, high aims that make a difference.
• For each activity ask: if we weren't doing this already, would we start?

cards.a: Concentration.
What you decide to stop or not start.

cards.q: Opportunity or problem: which guides priorities?
cards.a: Opportunity.

concepts.s: Decide few, fundamental things by a clear process: classify, set conditions, find what is right, act, and check.

x.b:
1. Drucker: Classify: is it generic (needs a rule or policy) or truly unique? Most problems are generic.
  2. Specifications: the boundary conditions the decision must meet.
  3. What is right before what is acceptable.
  4. Convert to action: who must know, who acts, with what.
  5. Feedback: check results against expectations firsthand.
  • Drucker: start from opinions, test them against facts, and insist on dissent; a decision with no disagreement has not been examined.
• Make few decisions, at the level of principle.
Trap: Treating a generic problem as unique and solving it again each time.

cards.a: Classify: generic or unique.
Otherwise you cannot tell a good compromise from a bad one.
Without it, alternatives were never examined.

concepts.s: Staff for what people do exceptionally well and make weaknesses irrelevant.

x.b:
• Drucker: staff from strength: ask what a person can do, not what they cannot.
  • Drucker: design jobs for normal people; a job that defeated two or three capable people in a row is impossible and must be redesigned.
  • Drucker: make productive the strengths of subordinates, peers, your boss and yourself.
• For each role, ask what this person does exceptionally well.
Trap: Hiring for absence of weakness: you get mediocrity.

cards.a: Staff from strength.

cards.q: What is an impossible job, by Drucker's test?
cards.a: One that defeated two or three capable people in a row; redesign it.
Use their strengths.

concepts.s: The ideal team player is humble, hungry and people-smart all at once, and missing any one causes predictable damage.

x.b:
• Lencioni: humble: little ego, shares credit (the most important); hungry: self-motivated, always wants to do more; smart: interpersonal sense, not intellect.
  • Lencioni: one virtue only: pawn (humble), bulldozer (hungry), charmer (smart).
  • Lencioni: two virtues: accidental mess-maker (no smart), lovable slacker (no hungry), skillful politician (no humble, the most dangerous).
• Use the model for hiring, assessing current staff, developing those short on a virtue, and embedding it in culture.

cards.a: Humble.
Skillful politician.
Accidental mess-maker.
Lovable slacker.

concepts.s: Design interviews to reveal humility, hunger and people sense, because standard interviews hide them.

x.b:
• Lencioni: debrief as a team right after each interview, on the three virtues.
  • Lencioni: use non-traditional settings that show real behavior.
  • Lencioni: ask key questions more than once and ask what others would say about them.
  • Lencioni: have candidates do real work.
  • Lencioni: tell candidates plainly you hire only humble, hungry, smart people; the wrong ones opt out.
  • Lencioni: don't take chances on a doubt.
• Listen for we over I and for credit given to others.

cards.a: Right after each interview, as a team.
Those who lack the virtues opt out.

cards.q: A lingering doubt about a candidate?
cards.a: Don't take the chance.

concepts.n: Write it down: plans, people, feedback
concepts.s: As a company scales, write down purpose, goals, how you work and how you judge performance, and review on a steady cadence.

x.b:
• Hughes Johnson: founding documents: mission, long-term goals, principles; teams write charters.
  • Hughes Johnson: an operating cadence for planning and reviewing goals and metrics, few clear goals repeated often.
  • Hughes Johnson: hire with a pipeline built ahead of need, honest role descriptions and a consistent rubric.
  • Hughes Johnson: self-awareness first: write a working-with-me guide on how you work and react, and share it.
  • Hughes Johnson: give direct feedback, say the hard thing, and base it on observed examples.
• Write your guide and your team's charter.

cards.a: Mission, long-term goals, principles.
A written guide to how you work and react, shared with your team.
A pipeline ahead of need, honest descriptions, one rubric.
